title: Shared letters, gaps allowed
hook: ABCBDAB and BDCABA share only 2 letters side by side. Allow gaps: how many now?

knows: a grid of smaller answers can solve edit distance (flaw-to-lawn)
doesNotKnow: that "what do two strings share, in order" is a different grid with a different cell rule
that a shared sequence may have gaps, so it can be longer than any shared block

misconception: The longest shared stretch is a block of letters side by side in both strings.
objective: The learner can fill the longest-common-subsequence grid for ABCBDAB and BDCABA (match: diagonal + 1; mismatch: larger of up and left), read 4 at the corner, trace back BCBA, and explain why it beats the longest shared block (2).

claims.text: The longest block of letters side by side in both ABCBDAB and BDCABA is 2 letters (AB or BD).
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14): every start pair compared letter by letter; longest common substring length 2, exactly AB and BD. Demo.tsx BLOCK recomputes the length. Unverified.

claims.text: Keeping order but allowing gaps, the longest sequence picked from both strings has 4 letters, and no 5-letter sequence is shared.
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14): grid fill gives 4 at the corner; brute force over all 127 subsequences of ABCBDAB and 63 of BDCABA gives maximum common length 4, with exactly three answers BCAB, BCBA, BDAB. Matches the brief (cs.algorithms.md #47). Unverified.

claims.text: Each cell asks whether its two letters match: if so, it is the diagonal + 1; if not, it is the larger of the cell above and the cell to the left.
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. section 14.4 (longest common subsequence, recurrence for c[i, j]); 3rd ed. section 15.4. Unverified.

claims.text: Each cell holds the length of the longest shared sequence of the first letters of each string, so the corner answers for the whole strings.
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. section 14.4: c[i, j] is the LCS length of the prefixes X_i and Y_j. Stage wording: 'Each cell: the best answer for the first letters of each string.' Unverified.

claims.text: Tracing back from the corner (diagonal on a match, otherwise to the larger neighbour, up on a tie) picks B, C, B, A: 4 letters in this order in both strings.
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14): traceback with ties going up visits matches at rows 2, 3, 4, 6 and columns 1, 3, 5, 6, spelling BCBA (same as CLRS PRINT-LCS tie rule). Demo.tsx PICKS recomputes it. Unverified.

claims.text: Diff tools that show what changed between two files are built on this idea.
claims.source: Hunt and McIlroy 1976, 'An algorithm for differential file comparison', Bell Labs CSTR 41 (Unix diff finds a longest common subsequence of lines); Myers 1986, 'An O(ND) difference algorithm and its variations', Algorithmica 1. 'Built on this idea' means LCS, not this exact grid fill. Unverified.

claims.text: The grid has 42 cells to fill: 7 rows by 6 columns.
claims.source: ABCBDAB has 7 letters and BDCABA has 6; 7 x 6 = 42 inner cells, the extra row and column of zeros are given. Unverified.

recall.question: In the shared-letters grid, the two letters for a cell do not match. What goes in the cell?
options: The larger of the cell above and the cell to the left
Zero, since the run of matching letters is broken
recall.why: A mismatch means one of the two letters is dropped, so the cell keeps the better of dropping it from either string: the larger of up and left. Gaps are allowed, so nothing resets to zero.
